review title: Civics and Criminal Justice Lifetime Movie for Kids
review: All that needs to be said about Eastwood's direction is already out there. Nevertheless, I'll agree that it was tight and moved the story forward with very little wasted scene time.The actors were OK as well. The fake southern drawl of the DA was a bit much, but otherwise the cast did a fine job with the script.And it's the script/story where I have problems. The story could have been made believable, but it simply wasn't. The number of coincidences, deus ex machina moments and plot rescue devices (the ex-cop's research on fender collisions for example) became too overwhelming for me to continue buying into the story. Further, I disagree with a lot of the reviews that say this paints a realistic picture of how people or juries work. It doesn't. While maybe it's close enough to reality for 8th graders in Civics class, it falls apart under the slightest of experienced scrutiny.I'll admit it's refreshing to not be assaulted with obnoxious CGI effects, a loud score and for a movie to rely mostly on human interaction and conversations. The direction and cinematography were very good, but the writing failed to do anything remotely memorable, unique or thought provoking for adults.

Superb casting with Nicholas Hoult & Toni Collett reunited 22 years after the Nick Hornby adaptation of About a Boy while Hugh Grant was in the screen next door in Heretic!Nicholas Hoult's acting deserves an oscar nomination as he struggles with his internal demons to do the right thingIt's a great story and along the lines of 12 angry men it focuses on the jury, the American selection process leaves a lot to be desired but this also focuses on the importance of good detective work & not to find your culprit then concentrate on evidence to convict that person without any proper investigation of any other possibilitiesJuror #4 is key to the plot , I never give spoilers as you know but perhaps it could been better written if the reveal & twist was withheld from the audience until the final quarter rather than it being in the first quarter that took away the suspense & mystery angle which would have made this a 10/10 must see and you leave feeling there were a plot holes thereIt's a story about turning a new leaf , it's about life & death and loss and the pursuit of justice regardless of evidence and jury peer pressure.Thought provoking with symbolic blind justice emblems throughoutBravo Clint 8/10 Pad. A.

This movie had the potential to be a good one. It's obviously very close to 12 Angry Men and a couple other jury movies. The acting was pretty well done and the cast easily drew me in to their world.For all there is to like about the movie, there are some gaps. They spend about 90 minutes building it up, creating tension between characters, only to never resolve or even fully explore that tension. They leave the focal point of the trial as an afterthought.But my biggest pet peeve is the ending. We spend all this time in your world, your vision. Then you leave the ending up to our interpretation. Pass.

I doubt that this case would ever have gone to trial. The only "witness" supposedly saw the suspect during a dark night, through heavy rain, from a couple of hundred feet away, right? If this case did make it to the courtroom, any halfway decent defense attorney would've knocked down the supposed validity of that witness without much trouble. There's nothing else to go on. The suspect followed her? How far? No one knows, which means that's of no value at all. If she was hit by a car, any autopsy would have shown this to have been the case, i.e. She was hit hard by a very large object... in other words, a vehicle, rather than a hand-held object. In summary, the direction, the actors and the production are all fine, but the whole film is a house built on a foundation that has no strength.

So decidedly un-Eastwood I was shocked when I realised who directed it. Rather than expose systematic flaws like you'd expect a libertarian like him to, he channels everything through literal characterisation and an individualistic moral quandary, and the Lifetime-esque scenes are clumsy accompaniments: Justin's phone almost giving away his tailing of Harold, his ongoing tilts with Marcus, every one of his awkward mishaps that threatens his innocence. The narrative set-up has potential but it's developed in such a generic manner that the cast feel like stock characters an AI was tasked with conjuring; the sassy black woman who just wants to get back to her kids, the jaded member of the community who's seen too much drug and gang violence, a savvy former cop, the up-and-coming district attorney hoping to clean up the streets, and the couple who are expecting and strained by the father's emotional absence. There's so little feel of the actual community beyond the courtroom and the one road that the crime takes place upon, but even leaving that locked room tension only reveals how bland the cinematic language employed here is. I doubt this would be engaging even if Hoult wasn't operating exclusively with the timid, nervous energy of a schoolboy (who really buys his monstrous, alcoholic past? Compare that to the imperfections of another late-era Eastwood in Richard Jewell, a similar but thornier premise that asks harder questions of the audience's perception of the protagonist). The ending confirms a simplistic view of how guilt interacts with comeuppance (in that it just happens as an entirely external event which resolves the former's every loose end). I'm reminded once again of the stark difference between the fates of a certain character from Infernal Affairs compared to its Western counterpart in Scorsese's The Departed. It feigns ambiguity but there's nothing open-ended about the justice it promotes, and nothing compelling about what he must confront.

This movie truly makes you reflect on life and the choices you make. It's a powerful story about facing tough decisions, taking responsibility for your actions, and the moral dilemmas that come with them. The main character struggles with whether to prioritize his family or another person, revealing the thin line between right and wrong. Everyone will have an opinion on his decision, and deep down, you'll sense what he should have done. In the end, the real question is: do you value your own life over another's? The answer lies in your personal values. This thoughtful film is also a fantastic conversation starter, prompting discussions on how others might act in the same situation.
